claim: The study sequenced 1181 SARS-CoV-2 samples to high depth in duplicate.
source: Here we describe the patterns of within-host diversity in 1181 SARS-CoV-2 samples sequenced to high depth in duplicate.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract describing the study design.

claim: 95.1% of samples show within-host mutations at detectable allele frequencies.
source: 95.1% of samples show within-host mutations at detectable allele frequencies.
evidence: Quantitative result from the analysis of the sequenced samples.

claim: The mutational spectra revealed strong strand asymmetries suggestive of damage or RNA editing of the plus strand, rather than replication errors.
source: Analyses of the mutational spectra revealed strong strand asymmetries suggestive of damage or RNA editing of the plus strand, rather than replication errors, dominating the accumulation of mutations during the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic.
evidence: Interpretation of mutational spectrum data presented in the study.

claim: Within- and between-host diversity show strong purifying selection, particularly against nonsense mutations.
source: Within- and between-host diversity show strong purifying selection, particularly against nonsense mutations.
evidence: Result from dN/dS analysis of the sequencing data.

claim: Recurrent within-host mutations display a spectrum and patterns of purifying selection more suggestive of mutational hotspots than recombination or convergent evolution.
source: Recurrent within-host mutations, many of which coincide with known phylogenetic homoplasies, display a spectrum and patterns of purifying selection more suggestive of mutational hotspots than recombination or convergent evolution.
evidence: Interpretation of recurrent mutation patterns observed in the data.

claim: Most samples result from infection by a single lineage based on allele frequencies.
source: While allele frequencies suggest that most samples result from infection by a single lineage, we identify multiple putative examples of co-infection.
evidence: Analysis of allele frequency distributions in the samples.

claim: Multiple putative examples of co-infection were identified.
source: While allele frequencies suggest that most samples result from infection by a single lineage, we identify multiple putative examples of co-infection.
evidence: Result from analysis of allele frequencies and comparison with consensus genomes.

claim: Mutational hotspots and rare cases of superinfection can confound transmission chain reconstruction analyses.
source: Integrating these results into an epidemiological inference framework, we find that while sharing of within-host variants between samples could help the reconstruction of transmission chains, mutational hotspots and rare cases of superinfection can confound these analyses.
evidence: Conclusion from epidemiological modeling using the within-host variant data.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has caused more than one million deaths as of the time of writing.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has caused global disruption and more than one million deaths (World Health Organization, 2020).
evidence: Cited from World Health Organization data.

claim: Over 100,000 viral genomes were sequenced by COG-UK as of December 2020.
source: Genomic analysis has yielded important insights into the origins and spread of the pandemic and has been an integral part of efforts to monitor viral transmission in the UK, with over 100,000 viral genomes sequenced as of December 2020 by COVID-19 Genomics UK (COG-UK), 2020.
evidence: Statement about the scale of genomic surveillance efforts.

claim: Deep sequencing data invariably reveal some level of within-host variation.
source: For purposes of genomic epidemiology, a consensus genome sequence is derived from each sample, but deep sequencing data invariably reveal some level of within-host variation (Lythgoe et al., 2020), and minor alleles are commonly filtered out prior to phylogenetic analysis (Meredith et al., 2020).
evidence: General observation supported by cited literature.

claim: It has been suggested that SARS-CoV-2 evolves within an infected host as a quasispecies.
source: It has been suggested that SARS-CoV-2, like SARS-CoV-1, evolves within an infected host as a quasispecies, with many mutations (within-host variants) arising which may be beneficial for the virus (Eigen, 1993; Holland et al., 1982; Lythgoe et al., 2020).
evidence: Hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: The study used the ARTIC protocol for SARS-CoV-2 genome sequencing.
source: To develop reliable methods for analysing within-host variation in the context of ongoing genomic epidemiological studies, we used the ARTIC protocol that is a common method used for SARS-CoV-2 genome sequencing by many labs around the world (DNA Pipelines R&D et al., 2020).
evidence: Description of the sequencing methodology used.

claim: Median sequencing coverage ranged from 998 to 49,025 read depth per replicate sample.
source: We generated sequencing data for 1181 samples in duplicate at a median sequencing coverage ranging from 998 to 49,025 read depth per replicate sample (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Quantitative description of sequencing depth achieved.

claim: As viral loads decrease, amplification biases and artefacts are more common and can impact within-host diversity analyses using RT-PCR protocols.
source: Overall, as viral loads decrease, amplification biases and artefacts are more common and can impact within-host diversity analyses using RT-PCR protocols (Zhao and Illingworth, 2019; Zanini et al., 2017; Illingworth et al., 2017).
evidence: Interpretation of the Ct value analysis supported by cited literature.

claim: ShearwaterML was used to reliably detect within-host variants with the ARTIC protocol.
source: To reliably detect within-host variants with the ARTIC protocol, we used ShearwaterML, an algorithm designed to detect variants at low allele frequencies.
evidence: Description of the computational method used for variant calling.

claim: ShearwaterML uses a base-specific overdispersed error model and calls mutations only when read support is statistically above background noise in other genomes.
source: ShearwaterML uses a base-specific overdispersed error model and calls mutations only when read support is statistically above background noise in other genomes (Gerstung et al., 2014; Martincorena et al., 2015; see Materials and methods).
evidence: Description of the algorithm's methodology from cited sources.

claim: A total of 18,888 putative variants were identified, including 7672 consensus variants and 11,216 within-host variants.
source: In total, we identified 18,888 putative variants (Supplementary file 2), including 7672 consensus variants (affecting 1063 sites) and 11,216 within-host variants (affecting 5545 sites).
evidence: Quantitative summary of variant calling results.

claim: Within-host variants included 7102 single-nucleotide substitutions, 3223 small deletions, 542 small insertions, and 349 putative multi-nucleotide variants.
source: Within-host variants included 7102 single-nucleotide substitutions, 3223 small deletions, 542 small insertions, and 349 putative multi-nucleotide variants (Materials and methods).
evidence: Breakdown of variant types identified in the analysis.

claim: The median number of within-host mutations detected per sample was 8.
source: Overall, within-host variation was detected in the vast majority of samples (95.1%), with a median of 8 within-host mutations detected per sample.
evidence: Statistical summary of within-host mutation counts.

claim: The mean standard deviation in within-host VAF at variable sites assuming a Bernoulli distribution was 0.12.
source: The mean standard deviation in within-host VAF at variable sites assuming a Bernoulli distribution of variants at each site was found to be 0.12 (Materials and methods).
evidence: Statistical measure calculated from the variant frequency data.

claim: C>U mutations account for 47.9% of all within-host point mutations.
source: C>U mutations account for 47.9% of all within-host point mutations compared to 5.3% for G>A mutations (C>U mutations in the minus strand), and G>U mutations account for 14.3% of mutations compared to 1.9% of C>A mutations (Materials and methods).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of mutational spectrum.

claim: G>A mutations account for 5.3% of all within-host point mutations.
source: C>U mutations account for 47.9% of all within-host point mutations compared to 5.3% for G>A mutations (C>U mutations in the minus strand), and G>U mutations account for 14.3% of mutations compared to 1.9% of C>A mutations (Materials and methods).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of mutational spectrum.

claim: G>U mutations account for 14.3% of all within-host point mutations.
source: C>U mutations account for 47.9% of all within-host point mutations compared to 5.3% for G>A mutations (C>U mutations in the minus strand), and G>U mutations account for 14.3% of mutations compared to 1.9% of C>A mutations (Materials and methods).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of mutational spectrum.

claim: C>A mutations account for 1.9% of all within-host point mutations.
source: C>U mutations account for 47.9% of all within-host point mutations compared to 5.3% for G>A mutations (C>U mutations in the minus strand), and G>U mutations account for 14.3% of mutations compared to 1.9% of C>A mutations (Materials and methods).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of mutational spectrum.

claim: The plus/minus strand ratio of the rate of C>U mutations is 9.6-fold.
source: Normalised for the genome sequence composition, the plus/minus strand ratios of the rates of C>U and G>U are 9.6-fold and 7-fold, respectively.
evidence: Calculated ratio from mutational spectrum data normalized for genome composition.

claim: The plus/minus strand ratio of the rate of G>U mutations is 7-fold.
source: Normalised for the genome sequence composition, the plus/minus strand ratios of the rates of C>U and G>U are 9.6-fold and 7-fold, respectively.
evidence: Calculated ratio from mutational spectrum data normalized for genome composition.

claim: The mutational spectrum of within-host variants closely resembles that of consensus variants.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Popa et al., 2020), the mutational spectrum of within-host variant closely resembles that of consensus variants (Figure 2).
evidence: Comparison of mutational spectra shown in Figure 2, consistent with cited literature.

claim: The expected number of differences between any two genomes within a sample is 0.83.
source: Across samples, we found the expected number of differences between any two genomes within a sample to be 0.83 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Calculated statistic from allele frequency data.

claim: Phylogenetic studies estimate a mutation rate in SARS-CoV-2 of 0.001 mutations/bp/year.
source: Phylogenetic studies estimate a mutation rate in SARS-CoV-2 of 0.001 mutations/bp/year (Fauver et al., 2020) or 0.082 mutations/genome/day.
evidence: Mutation rate estimate from cited phylogenetic study.

claim: The observed within-host mutation load is consistent with the expected acquisition of mutations during a relatively short span of several days.
source: Thus, the observed within-host mutation load would be consistent with the expected acquisition of mutations during a relatively short span of several days.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of observed diversity with known mutation rate.

claim: The number of within-host variants tended to increase over time in individuals with multiple samples.
source: Overall, the number of within-host variants tended to increase over time and this trend was significant using a Poisson mixed model to control for host-specific effects (p=0.007; Figure 3B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of longitudinal samples with p-value reported.

claim: No change in the consensus genome sequence was observed in any of the individuals from whom multiple samples were collected.
source: In contrast, we observed no change in the consensus genome sequence in any of the individuals from whom multiple samples were collected.
evidence: Result from analysis of longitudinal samples.

claim: dN/dS ratios for consensus variants are under clear purifying selection.
source: As expected, dN/dS ratios for consensus variants are under clear purifying selection (Figure 4A), with particularly strong selection against nonsense mutations.
evidence: Result from dN/dS analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Within-host variants reaching moderately high allele frequencies (VAF > 10%) display similarly strong purifying selection against missense and nonsense mutations as consensus variants.
source: Within-host variants reaching moderately high allele frequencies (VAF > 10%) display similarly strong purifying selection against missense and nonsense mutations as consensus variants (Figure 4A), while within-host variants at low allele frequencies appear to be under more relaxed purifying selection, as it may be expected.
evidence: Result from dN/dS analysis stratified by allele frequency.

claim: Within-host variants at low allele frequencies appear to be under more relaxed purifying selection.
source: Within-host variants reaching moderately high allele frequencies (VAF > 10%) display similarly strong purifying selection against missense and nonsense mutations as consensus variants (Figure 4A), while within-host variants at low allele frequencies appear to be under more relaxed purifying selection, as it may be expected.
evidence: Result from dN/dS analysis stratified by allele frequency.

claim: Selection within hosts, rather than during transmission, may explain a considerable fraction of the extent of purifying selection observed in consensus sequences.
source: Overall, the similarity of dN/dS ratios for consensus and moderate-VAF within-host variants suggests that selection within hosts, rather than during transmission, may explain a considerable fraction of the extent of purifying selection observed in consensus sequences.
evidence: Inference from comparison of dN/dS ratios between consensus and within-host variants.

claim: Within-host variation is observed in at least 5 samples at 215 sites within the SARS-CoV-2 genome.
source: Within-host variation is observed in at least 5 (0.4%) of our samples at 215 sites within the SARS-CoV-2 genome (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Quantitative summary of recurrent within-host variant sites.

claim: Most recurrent within-host variants occur across lineages, independently of the genomic background of fixed variants present in a sample.
source: Instead, we find that most recurrent within-host variants occur across lineages, independently of the genomic background of fixed variants present in a sample (Figure 4E).
evidence: Analysis of recurrent variants across phylogenetic lineages.

claim: Most recurrent within-host variants are likely to represent hypermutable sites rather than convergent positive selection.
source: This suggests that most recurrent within-host variants are likely to represent hypermutable sites rather than convergent positive selection.
evidence: Inference from the high proportion of synonymous mutations and dN/dS analysis of recurrent variants.

claim: The spike glycoprotein mutation D614G was rapidly increasing in frequency throughout the world at the time these samples were collected.
source: A plausible example of positive selection is the spike glycoprotein mutation D614G, which was rapidly increasing in frequency throughout the world at the time these samples were collected: within-host variation at this position appears in 27 of our samples, with the D614G allele often present at high allele frequencies.
evidence: Observation of D614G variant in the dataset combined with knowledge of its global spread.

claim: Within-host variation at the D614G position appears in 27 samples.
source: A plausible example of positive selection is the spike glycoprotein mutation D614G, which was rapidly increasing in frequency throughout the world at the time these samples were collected: within-host variation at this position appears in 27 of our samples, with the D614G allele often present at high allele frequencies.
evidence: Quantitative observation from the dataset.

claim: The samples represent a broad range of the SARS-CoV-2 genetic diversity found in the UK at that time.
source: This showed that our samples represent a broad range of the SARS-CoV-2 genetic diversity found in the UK at that time and that the diversity observed among our samples was not primarily driven by geographical location.
evidence: Result from phylogenetic analysis of samples in context of COG-UK dataset.

claim: The diversity observed among samples was not primarily driven by geographical location.
source: This showed that our samples represent a broad range of the SARS-CoV-2 genetic diversity found in the UK at that time and that the diversity observed among our samples was not primarily driven by geographical location.
evidence: Result from phylogenetic and geographic analysis.

claim: Within-host variants are often shared between samples that are distant on the consensus phylogeny.
source: This confirmed that within-host variants are often shared between samples that are distant on the consensus phylogeny.
evidence: Observation from phylogenetic analysis of shared within-host variants.

claim: Recent studies have suggested that the bottleneck in SARS-CoV-2 transmission can be on the order of 10²–10³ virions.
source: While recent studies have suggested that the bottleneck in SARS-CoV-2 transmission can be on the order of 102–103 virions, they also identified substantial overlaps in the fraction of shared minority variants between samples unrelated by close transmission (Popa et al., 2020; Mara and Chu, 2020).
evidence: Summary of findings from cited studies.

claim: A re-analysis of the Austrian data estimated much smaller bottleneck on the order of 1–3 virions.
source: Indeed, a re-analysis of the Austrian data estimated much smaller bottleneck on the order of 1–3 virions (Martin Michael and Katia, 2021).
evidence: Result from cited re-analysis study.

claim: 36 putative co-infected samples were identified.
source: This resulted in 36 putative co-infected samples, with a representative example shown in Figure 6A.
evidence: Result from linear model analysis to identify mixed infections.

claim: A weak correlation with transmission probability was found for shared within-host variants of high allele frequency.
source: A weak correlation with transmission probability was found for shared within-host variants of high allele frequency, but not for those of low allele frequency.
evidence: Result from transcluster analysis of transmission probability.

claim: Much of the correlation between shared within-host variants and transmission probability was potentially driven by co-infections.
source: Figure 6C indicates that the remaining within-host variants no longer correlate as well with the probability of direct transmission, suggesting that much of the correlation observed previously was potentially driven by co-infections.
evidence: Result from re-analysis after excluding putative co-infections.

claim: The prevalence of infection within hospitals during the first 'wave' of the COVID-19 pandemic was often considerably higher than in the community.
source: The prevalence of infection within hospitals, particularly during the first 'wave' of the COVID-19 pandemic was often considerably higher than in the community with up to 50% of the consultant A and E workforce at one Welsh hospital testing positive in April 2020 (Black et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited data on hospital infection rates.

claim: Approximately 6% of the UK population had been infected with SARS-CoV-2 by the end of June 2020.
source: This contrasts with the finding that approximately 6% of the UK population had been infected with SARS-CoV-2 by the end of June (Ward et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited population-level infection data.

claim: 41% of 138 patients in Wuhan were found to have contracted SARS-CoV-2 in hospital.
source: Within-hospital transmission was also common in the early stages of the outbreak in Wuhan, with 41% of 138 patients found to have contracted SARS-CoV-2 in hospital (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited data on nosocomial transmission in Wuhan.

claim: Two randomly chosen genomes within a sample differ by 0.83 variants on average.
source: By analysing the frequency of variants within individual samples, we estimate that two randomly chosen genomes within a sample differ by 0.83 variants on average.
evidence: Calculated estimate from allele frequency data.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 genome is known to acquire approximately one mutation every 2 weeks.
source: Since most of these samples were probably collected more than a week after the time of infection, and since the SARS-CoV-2 genome is known to acquire approximately one mutation every 2 weeks, these findings are broadly consistent with the hypothesis that within-host variation is largely due to the accumulation of de novo mutations within the host or, at least, in the span of a few days.
evidence: Statement of known mutation rate used for comparison.

claim: Increased numbers of within-host variants have been observed in immunocompromised patients.
source: Increased numbers of within-host variants have also been observed in immunocompromised patients: consistent with the acquisition of de novo mutations within the host (Siqueira Juliana et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited observation from study of immunocompromised patients.

claim: Within-host variants have a similar mutational spectrum to the consensus variants that define between-host variation.
source: These data show that within-host variants have a similar mutational spectrum to the consensus variants that define between-host variation.
evidence: Summary of mutational spectrum analysis.

claim: Both within-host and consensus variants are characterised by clear purifying selection.
source: Both are characterised by clear purifying selection, as would be expected if virions with disadvantageous mutations failed to survive or propagate within the host.
evidence: Result from dN/dS analysis with biological interpretation.

claim: The mutational spectrum of SARS-CoV-2 exhibits a near complete asymmetry between the plus and minus strands.
source: Strikingly, the mutational spectrum of SARS-CoV-2 exhibits a near complete asymmetry between the plus and minus strands and is dominated by C>U and G>U mutations.
evidence: Observation from mutational spectrum analysis.

claim: The spectrum observed is very different to that of APOBEC mutagenesis in DNA from human cells.
source: Whilst current knowledge of the mutational spectrum of APOBEC enzymes on RNA molecules is insufficient to assess the likelihood that they actively contribute to SARS-CoV-2 evolution, we note that the spectrum observed is very different to that of APOBEC mutagenesis in DNA from human cells.
evidence: Comparison of observed spectrum with known APOBEC signature.

claim: Direct damage of cytosine and guanine bases could be consistent with the observed spectrum of C>U and G>U changes in SARS-CoV-2.
source: Instead, direct damage of cytosine and guanine bases could also be consistent with the observed spectrum of C>U and G>U changes in SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: Proposed alternative explanation for the observed mutational spectrum.

claim: Many of the within-host variants identified are shared between infected individuals located on distant branches of the consensus phylogeny.
source: Many of the within-host variants that we have identified are shared between infected individuals located on distant branches of the consensus phylogeny, and this is congruent with previous reports that the SARS-CoV-2 consensus phylogeny has many homoplasies that also appear as within-host variants (Lythgoe et al., 2021).
evidence: Observation from phylogenetic analysis, consistent with cited literature.

claim: The sharing of within-host variants across distant phylogenetic branches is largely due to recurrent mutation.
source: It appears likely that this is largely due to recurrent mutation although co-infection between lineages could also be a relevant factor in high transmission settings.
evidence: Interpretation of the pattern of shared variants with acknowledgment of alternative explanation.

claim: The vast majority of samples appear to comprise a single lineage.
source: The vast majority of our samples appear to comprise a single lineage, but we find evidence of putative co-infection by multiple lineages in approximately 3–4% of samples, which is likely an underestimate of the extent of co-infection in our dataset.
evidence: Result from analysis of allele frequencies and mixture modeling.

claim: Approximately 3–4% of samples show evidence of putative co-infection by multiple lineages.
source: The vast majority of our samples appear to comprise a single lineage, but we find evidence of putative co-infection by multiple lineages in approximately 3–4% of samples, which is likely an underestimate of the extent of co-infection in our dataset.
evidence: Quantitative result from mixture modeling analysis.

claim: In other viral and bacterial diseases, within-host variants provide a valuable source of information for the inference of transmission chains.
source: In other viral and bacterial diseases, within-host variants provide a valuable source of information for the inference of transmission chains (De Maio et al., 2018; Chris et al., 2017; Worby et al., 2017; Arias et al., 2016) and have been shown to improve the accuracy of inferences based on consensus genomes (Worby et al., 2014; Hall et al., 2015; De Maio et al., 2016; Campbell et al., 2018).
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple cited studies on other pathogens.

claim: Initial estimates suggested that the transmission bottleneck for SARS-CoV-2 may be large.
source: In the case of SARS-CoV-2, initial estimates suggested that the transmission bottleneck may be large (Lythgoe et al., 2020; Popa et al., 2020).
evidence: Summary of initial findings from cited studies.

claim: Revised estimates suggest that a much smaller bottleneck is likely similar to that seen in Influenza.
source: However, revised estimates suggest that a much smaller bottleneck is likely similar to that seen in Influenza (Lythgoe et al., 2021).
evidence: Summary of revised findings from cited study.

claim: There is considerable genetic diversity in the SARS-CoV-2 viral populations within individual hosts.
source: In summary, these data show that there is considerable genetic diversity in the SARS-CoV-2 viral populations within individual hosts.
evidence: Summary conclusion from the overall analysis.

claim: Within-host diversity seems consistent with the accumulation of de novo mutations during the course of infection but can also result from co-infection with different lineages.
source: Within-host diversity seems consistent with the accumulation of de novo mutations during the course of infection but can also result from co-infection with different lineages.
evidence: Summary interpretation of the sources of within-host diversity.

claim: Analysis of within-host variation could potentially be used to improve the inference of transmission chains, but this approach requires caution because of the confounding effects of recurrent mutation and unrelated episodes of superinfection.
source: Analysis of within-host variation could potentially be used to improve the inference of transmission chains, but this approach requires caution because of the confounding effects of recurrent mutation and unrelated episodes of superinfection.
evidence: Conclusion from the epidemiological analysis with caveats identified.

claim: The 1181 samples were taken as a random subset from a larger prospective study into SARS-CoV-2 infections at Cambridge University Hospitals.
source: The 1181 samples were taken as a random subset from a larger prospective study into SARS-CoV-2 infections at Cambridge University Hospitals National Health Service Foundation Trust (CUH; Cambridge, UK), a secondary care provider and tertiary referral centre in the East of England (Meredith et al., 2020; Hamilton et al., 2020).
evidence: Description of sample selection and study design.

claim: Two libraries were generated from two aliquots of each sample with separate RT, PCR amplification, and library preparation steps.
source: Two libraries were then generated from two aliquots of each sample with separate RT, PCR amplification, and library preparation steps in order to evaluate the quality and reproducibility of within-host variant calls.
evidence: Description of the experimental design for technical replication.

claim: The ARTIC protocol v3 was used for library preparation.
source: The ARTIC protocol v3 was used for library preparation (a full description of the protocol used is available at http://dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.be3wjgpe).
evidence: Description of the sequencing protocol used.

claim: Alignment was performed using the ARTIC Illumina nextflow pipeline.
source: Alignment was performed using the ARTIC Illumina nextflow pipeline available from https://github.com/connor-lab/ncov2019-artic-nf (Bull, 2020; copy archived at swh:1:rev:8af5152cf7107c3a369b996f5bad3473d329050c).
evidence: Description of the bioinformatics pipeline used.

claim: The pipeline trims primer and adapter sequences prior to alignment to the reference genome using bwa.
source: The pipeline trims primer and adapter sequences prior to alignment to the reference genome using bwa (MN908947.3) (Li and Durbin, 2009).
evidence: Description of the alignment methodology.

claim: Variants were called separately for each set of duplicates.
source: Variants were called separately for each set of duplicates.
evidence: Description of the variant calling procedure.

claim: Two samples were excluded as they had an unusually high number of low-frequency variants unlikely to be of biological origin.
source: Two samples were excluded, as they had an unusually high number of low-frequency variants unlikely to be of biological origin, leaving 1179 samples for analysis, comprising 1121 infected individuals of whom 49 had multiple samples.
evidence: Description of quality control filtering.

claim: The study included 1121 infected individuals of whom 49 had multiple samples.
source: Two samples were excluded, as they had an unusually high number of low-frequency variants unlikely to be of biological origin, leaving 1179 samples for analysis, comprising 1121 infected individuals of whom 49 had multiple samples.
evidence: Description of the study cohort composition.

claim: The allele frequency for each variant was taken as the frequency of the variant in the combined set of reads from both replicates.
source: The allele frequency for each variant was taken as the frequency of the variant in the combined set of reads from both replicates.
evidence: Description of how allele frequencies were calculated.

claim: Consensus variants were defined as those present in the majority of reads aligned to a position of the reference genome.
source: Within each sample, we classified variant calls as 'consensus' if they were present in the majority of reads aligned to a position of the reference genome or as within-host variants otherwise.
evidence: Definition of consensus variants used in the analysis.

claim: The plus strand is the infectious genome, exported from the replication organelles into the cytoplasm.
source: The plus strand is the infectious genome, exported from the replication organelles, where minus molecules reside, into the cytoplasm (Wolff et al., 2020), translated, packaged into particles, and transmitted between cells and hosts.
evidence: Statement about viral biology supported by citation.

claim: The plus strand is present within cells in much larger numbers than the minus strand.
source: The plus strand is also present within cells in much larger numbers than the minus strand (Sawicki et al., 2007).
evidence: Statement about viral replication supported by citation.

claim: APOBEC cytosine deaminase enzymes cause cytosine to uracil transitions.
source: Two families of RNA-editing enzymes in particular have been speculated to contribute to the mutational spectrum of SARS-CoV-2, APOBEC cytosine deaminase enzymes causing cytosine to uracil transitions and ADAR enzymes causing adenosine-to-inosine changes (A>G/U>C mutations) (Di Giorgio et al., 2020; Simmonds, 2020).
evidence: Description of enzyme activity from cited literature.

claim: ADAR enzymes cause adenosine-to-inosine changes (A>G/U>C mutations).
source: Two families of RNA-editing enzymes in particular have been speculated to contribute to the mutational spectrum of SARS-CoV-2, APOBEC cytosine deaminase enzymes causing cytosine to uracil transitions and ADAR enzymes causing adenosine-to-inosine changes (A>G/U>C mutations) (Di Giorgio et al., 2020; Simmonds, 2020).
evidence: Description of enzyme activity from cited literature.

claim: The activity of APOBEC3A and 3B enzymes in human cancers is distinctly characterised by a strong sequence context, leading to C>T and C>G changes almost solely at TpC sites.
source: While the mutational spectrum induced by all APOBEC enzymes is not fully understood, the activity of the better-understood APOBEC3A and 3B enzymes in human cancers is distinctly characterised by a strong sequence context, leading to C>T and C>G changes almost solely at TpC sites (Alexandrov et al., 2020).
evidence: Description of APOBEC mutational signature from cited cancer genomics study.

claim: Spontaneous cytosine deamination would cause C>U transitions.
source: For example, spontaneous cytosine deamination would cause C>U transitions while oxidation of guanine bases could explain G>U transversions (Krokan et al., 2002).
evidence: Statement about DNA damage mechanisms supported by citation.

claim: Oxidation of guanine bases could explain G>U transversions.
source: For example, spontaneous cytosine deamination would cause C>U transitions while oxidation of guanine bases could explain G>U transversions (Krokan et al., 2002).
evidence: Statement about DNA damage mechanisms supported by citation.

claim: Both cytosine deamination and guanine oxidation are common mutagenic processes on DNA in human cells.
source: Both forms of damage are common mutagenic processes on DNA in human cells (Helleday et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about DNA damage in human cells supported by citation.

claim: The study used dNdScv package to calculate dN/dS ratios.
source: To study the extent of selection acting on within-host variants and consensus variants, we calculated dN/dS ratios using the dNdScv package (Materials and methods).
evidence: Description of the analytical method used.

claim: dNdScv uses a Poisson framework allowing for complex substitution models including context dependence, strand asymmetry, non-equilibrium sequence composition, and estimation of dN/dS ratios for missense and nonsense mutations separately.
source: dNdScv uses a Poisson framework allowing for complex substitution models including context dependence, strand asymmetry, non-equilibrium sequence composition, and estimation of dN/dS ratios for missense and nonsense mutations separately.
evidence: Description of the dNdScv method capabilities.

claim: This model is particularly suitable for datasets with low mutation density in lowly recombining or non-recombining populations.
source: This model is particularly suitable for datasets with low mutation density in lowly recombining or non-recombining populations, as it is the case in SARS-CoV-2 genomic data Martincorena et al., 2017.
evidence: Statement about the suitability of the method for SARS-CoV-2 data.

claim: Variable sites are dominated by those seen at the third codon position.
source: Variable sites are dominated by those seen at the third codon position similar to that observed in Dyrdak et al., 2019.
evidence: Observation from Figure 1—figure supplement 4, consistent with cited literature.

claim: The use of replicates and a base-specific statistical error model for calling within-host diversity reduces the risk of erroneous calls at low allele frequencies.
source: The use of replicates and a base-specific statistical error model for calling within-host diversity reduces the risk of erroneous calls at low allele frequencies.
evidence: Statement about the methodological approach to reduce errors.

claim: A slight increase in the number of within-host diversity calls was noticed for samples with high Ct values.
source: We noticed a slight increase in the number of within-host diversity calls for samples with high Ct values, which may be caused by a small number of errors or by the amplification of rare alleles and that could inflate within-host diversity estimates (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; McCrone and Lauring, 2016).
evidence: Observation from the data with potential explanations.

claim: The mutational spectrum of within-host mutations closely resembles that of consensus mutations.
source: As described in the following sections, this includes the fact that the mutational spectrum of within-host mutations closely resembles that of consensus mutations and the observation of a clear signal of negative selection on within-host mutations, as demonstrated by dN/dS and by an enrichment of within-host mutations at third codon positions (Dyrdak et al., 2019; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Summary of evidence supporting the quality of within-host mutation calls.
